summary: Suggests a new procedure for assigning subnet numbers within a network. Using it is purely a local matter and does not affect other networks. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When splitting a neighborhood into blocks, this suggests a numbering plan that is easier to adjust later.

questions: how to assign subnet numbers flexibly
how to avoid renumbering subnets when growing
how to split a network without renumbering
subtitle: A flexible numbering technique that lets networks grow without renumbering existing machines.

tldr.problem: When networks grow, administrators often must renumber subnets or leave them inefficiently spaced, wasting address space and requiring changes to many machines.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC proposes assigning subnet numbers starting from the most significant bits (left) and host numbers starting from the least significant bits (right), leaving a growth area in the middle that can expand in either direction as needed.
tldr.outcome: Networks can add more subnets or more hosts to existing subnets without renumbering any machines, if routers support variable-length subnet masks.

facts.label: Address space
facts.value: Works with any IP version using subnet masks

today: RFC 1219 is an Informational RFC that is still relevant. It describes a subnet assignment technique that allows networks to grow flexibly. The technique is not required by any standard but is purely optional and local; modern routing protocols support the VLSM requirement.

sections.title: The Problem with Fixed Subnet Plans
sections.content:
RFC 950 introduced subnetting, which divides a network address into a subnet part and a host part using a subnet mask. This allows a network to be split into multiple smaller networks, improving routing efficiency. However, when an administrator sets up subnets, they must guess how many hosts each subnet will eventually need. If a subnet grows beyond that estimate, it must be renumbered—a painful process that means changing addresses on many machines, updating DNS records, and modifying configuration files.

For example, if subnet B runs out of address space, moving to a new subnet number means renumbering all hosts in B, even though address space might exist elsewhere in the network that could be used if only the numbering were different.
sections.plainLanguage: When you first divide a street into blocks, you have to guess how many houses will fit on each block. If Block 2 fills up and you need to add more houses, you have to renumber all the existing houses in Block 2. That is painful and error-prone.

sections.title: Mirror-Image Counting for Subnet Numbers
sections.content:
RFC 1219 proposes a different assignment strategy. Instead of assigning consecutive subnet numbers in normal order (1, 2, 3...), it uses mirror-image counting: subnet numbers are assigned from the most significant bit (leftmost) working toward the least significant bit (rightmost). At the same time, host numbers within each subnet are assigned from the least significant bit (rightmost) working left in the normal way.

The technique divides address bits into three categories: s-bits (subnet bits, assigned from the left), h-bits (host bits, assigned from the right), and g-bits (growth bits in the middle, initially zero). As more hosts are needed in a subnet, g-bits become h-bits. As more subnets are needed, g-bits become s-bits. Crucially, no existing host address ever changes—the growth happens in the previously unused g-bits.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of numbering all subnets first and then numbering hosts, you number subnet blocks from one end and host numbers from the other end, leaving the middle open. When you need more of either, you expand from the middle without disturbing what is already there.

sections.title: The Assignment Algorithm
sections.content:
RFC 1219 provides detailed algorithms for initializing the system and adding or removing subnets and hosts. When a new subnet is added, the algorithm assigns it the lowest unassigned subnet number in mirror-image order, then labels which bits are s-bits, h-bits, and g-bits. If an existing subnet is affected (its bits collide with the new subnet in a way that requires clarification), that subnet's g-bits are promoted to s-bits—but the hosts in that subnet are never renumbered.

Similarly, when a new host is added to a subnet, it claims one of the unused g-bits. If the last g-bit is claimed by a host, the address authority assigning subnets must be notified so subnets do not mistakenly reuse that bit. The technique requires that routers support variable-length subnet masks (VLSM), because different subnets may have different subnet mask lengths.
sections.plainLanguage: The algorithm is like a smart rule: when you add a new subnet, you number it in a special counting order from left to right. When you add a new host, you number it normally but starting from the right. If the two approaches meet in the middle, you just tell the person managing subnets so they know where the boundary is now.

sections.title: A Class C Network Example
sections.content:
The RFC demonstrates the technique with a concrete example using a Class C network (8 bits available for subnets and hosts). Starting with three subnets A (binary 10), B (binary 01), and C (binary 110), each with 6 available host addresses, the example shows how a fourth subnet D (binary 001) can be added without changing any existing addresses. The subnet masks can be chosen so that both hosts and subnets have room to grow without hitting each other.

When a fifth subnet is later added, some g-bits must be converted to s-bits for existing subnets to avoid numbering collisions. However, the example shows that machines in existing subnets only need to learn about the new subnet mask—their own addresses stay the same. This flexibility, combined with the ability to change masks without renumbering hosts, is the key advantage over traditional fixed subnet planning.
sections.plainLanguage: With the first three subnets numbered in mirror order, you can add a fourth without disturbing them. When you add a fifth, you might need to adjust how the middle bits are divided, but no existing house number changes.

sections.title: Router Support and Coordination
sections.content:
RFC 1219 requires that intra-domain routing protocols support multiple different subnet masks on the same network (VLSM). Classic routing protocols like RIP did not support this, but newer protocols such as OSPF do. When a new subnet consumes the last growth bit, the address authority managing subnets and the address authority managing hosts must coordinate to avoid assigning the same bit to both functions simultaneously.

The technique does not require any changes to Internet standards or to IP itself. It is purely a local matter—each organization can choose to adopt it or not. The RFC notes that this technique is not entirely new but had not been widely documented or implemented at the time of publication. With the emergence of routing protocols that support variable-length masks, the technique became more practical and worth formalizing in an RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: The routers running your network need to be smart enough to handle subnets of different sizes. If they are, you can use this technique. If not, you are stuck with the old method of rigid, fixed-size subnets.
